page_title: Focus day 22-09-01 - Semantic Release Versioning and GitHub Runners
content: While it s partly the solution architects  and teams  responsibility areas, it is evident that some teams would benefit from guidance and assistance with patterns on how to address proper versioning Semantic versioning, as a concept, may seem pretty straight-forward, but when adding automation, changelogs and various pipelines the complexity rises

page_title: Focus day 22-09-01 - Semantic Release Versioning and GitHub Runners
content: For example, there may be 5 pull-requests merged for a release; one with a major breaking change, one with a minor change, and three with patch updates only How is this tracked We also need to take into consideration that some teams have abandoned npm semver, as it did not fit their release model

page_title: Focus day 22-09-01 - Semantic Release Versioning and GitHub Runners
content: One idea that I m currently thinking of is: Use pull-request titles to denote the change (major, minor, patch) Each single commit has no relevance; it is the totality (like a squashed commit) that counts When the pull-request is closed, and merged, (not abandoned), create a tag with major, minor, and patch To avoid concurrency issues we add a unique build number to the tag; e.g., v1.5.2.44 Then, when creating a release candidate, the correct (and latest tag) already exists, so the input field is only optional (if one would like to override the latest tag)

content: This page is out of date For any API contract testing, it is advisable to use the PACT framework approach It has been tried a couple of times within IPEX, but not yet fully applied anywhere Contact for an intro.What is Contract API testing?The benefit of Contract API testing specially consumer driven is that you get to test the best of both worlds

page_title: IPEX Contract API testing approach and recommendation
content: You can test using Mocks (quick, cheap, fast to implement) and using real time dependency with an E2E fully deployed environment.To put it simply   with contract testing, you work with mocks that represent the agreed-upon API contract between the services, but also, the services (producers) that provide the API for consumption have to uphold that API contract that is used in those mocks

page_title: IPEX Contract API testing approach and recommendation
content: The contract is enforced in their CI so they can t break the API and go to production.SO a combined approach of both consumer and producer driven API testing is highly recommended, specially in today s world of complex SOAs, micro-services driven architectures.Test Strategy:4 Key players: Consumer, Producer, Contracts and BrokerRole: Consumer interacts with dependent service through an API provided by the producer

page_title: IPEX Contract API testing approach and recommendation
content: The interaction can be done via another back-end API provided by a different producer or the same producer Or the interaction can be done by a front-end browser version.Contract plays a KEY role in defining how the request response model should look like That means it defines the agreement between the consumer and producer on how the API should behave.Producer develops and exposes the service

page_title: Skapa as Upstream source in Azure Artifacts
content: Answer- It doesn t go in order, the feed makes calls to all of the up streams to find all versions The order is used to determine where to get the package from once the server has all responses

page_title: Skapa as Upstream source in Azure Artifacts
content: In other words, the downstream feed asks all upstream feeds "Hey, do you have this?" and then gives preference on where to download the package based on the order and the version that you want.In this case, if you are trying to download package foo, and foo exists ONLY in npmjs then you get a 502 because:Feed asks all upstreams for the package metadata (aka, what versions do they have?)Custom public upstream returns a 401 because the package doesn t existServer says "well that s not a valid response from the upstream"Server return 502 Skapa is looking into moving from Verdaccio so adding Skapa as an upstream source might be feasible in the future

ConsiderationsThere are some considerations to keep in mind when doing this investigation.Can one tool fit all projects independent of things like source control selection, BitBucket, GitHub, other?How easy is it to setup What does the setup require

How is a defined and created?How easy is it to extend, create and share custom build steps between projects?Is it possible to integrate easy with Jira?Can test results be visualised in good standard way without a lot of effort?OptionsThis evaluation focus around two different platforms and what benefit and drawbacks the both have and how they fit IPEX project structure.Bitbucket PipelinesAzure DevOpsBitbucket PipelinesBitbucket pipelines are built into Bitbucket and work inside your Bitbucket project.Source ControlBitbucket pipelines works best together with Bitbucket as your source control

It would be possible to use a different source, such as GitHub, however that would require triggering the pipelines through web-hooks and it would require you to check out the code from GitHub your self in a custom pipe There is no out of the box setup for this kind of scenario.Setup and creationTo get started with Bitbucket pipelines you create a bitbucket-pipelines.yml file in your repository

To get started with Bitbucket pipelines you create a bitbucket-pipelines.yml file in your repository This file is yaml file with configuration for your pipeline It contain different kind of build, deployments, steps, pipes, and more

It configures what should be triggered by different actions in the repository, such as pull-requests, merges, and more.The configuration file can be very long and complex, depending on your project, the good thing is it would be possible to create a template with standard configuration and share that among IPEX projects

Giving each new project a flying start.CustomisationBitbucket pipelines is fairly easy to customise and create custom build steps Bitbucket uses what is called Pipes which is basically a Docker container running your task There already exists many Pipes from 3:rd party tools like JFrog Artifactory and more

Pipes can be published and pulled in from any Docker registry making it very easy to share custom pipes between projects.Jira integrationBitbucket pipelines integrate really good with Jira, after the initial setup it will be possible to view things like deployment history for specifik issues from Jira This require that each commit in Bitbucket is taged with a Jira issue number
It also enables the possibility to work with Jira issues, updating them, directly from Bitbucket.ArtifactsEach build step can easy define artifacts that should be available to the next step to use

Artifacts are also downloadable from the build step in the Pipeline, these are kept for 7 days, if longer retention is needed they should be uploaded to S3 or similar.Test reportsTest reports in any xUnit-compatible format will automatically be picked up and visualised, if they are stored in any of the predefined locations supported locations can be found hereDeployment trackingIt s possible to create and specify deployments to different environments, test, staging, production, and more

ble to create and specify deployments to different environments, test, staging, production, and more Pipeline will automatically track what commit has been released to what environment If the commit message contain one or many Jira issue numbers it s possible to do the same tracking directly from Jira

Azure DevOpsSource ControlAzure Devops Pipelines integrates with several source control services, including GitHub and Bitbucket Cloud Setup and creationThe setup of Azure Pipelines differ depending on your source repository The process for setting it up for GitHub is rather easy, check the quick start guide

When you have your pipeline connected to the repository you can modify and update the azure-pipelines.yml config file It would then be possible to create standard IPEX configurations that can be shared between projects.CustomisationTasks are the foundation of the pipeline There are many tasks ready out of the box to use in any pipeline
are the foundation of the pipeline There are many tasks ready out of the box to use in any pipeline It s possible to create custom tasks that can be shared across the organisation

It would be possible to create and share custom IPEX tasks to fullfil parts needed in the pipeline.Jira integrationIt s possible to integrate Jira with Azure pipelines to view associated issues in Azure pipelines and also see builds and deployments in Jira The Jira integration need to be installed and configured.ArtifactsIn Azure pipeline there are several types of artifacts

need to be installed and configured.ArtifactsIn Azure pipeline there are several types of artifacts Some types move between build steps and some are designed to be published This is something you define in your pipeline Check the documentation for a full list of artifact types.Test reportsAzure DevOps   Pipelines has an excellent test result reporting built in

artifact types.Test reportsAzure DevOps   Pipelines has an excellent test result reporting built in You get great visualisation of test runs for each build The reporting regarding other things like code coverage and more is really good See documentation for details.Deployment trackingIt s possible to visualise the status of the release pipelines, things like release to different environments

Tracking Jira issues should be possible if Jira has been integrated.RecommendationRight now it s hard to get one tool to rule them all.The recommendation would be to use Bitbucket pipelines for projects using Bitbucket as the source control and to use Azure Pipelines for projects using GitHub
